lesson_title: Fair Shares with Thirds and Sixths
big_idea: Sharing fairly between 3 friends gives thirds. Between 6 friends gives sixths.
learning_intention: We are learning to share collections fairly between 2, 3, 4, or 6 friends, and to recognise that one third equals two sixths of the same whole.
student_learning_goal: I can share a small collection fairly between 2, 3, 4, or 6 friends, and tell that one third equals two sixths.
success_criteria: I can share a collection fairly into equal groups for 2, 3, 4, or 6 friends.
I can split one item into thirds or sixths if there is a leftover.
I can show that one third equals two sixths of the same whole.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Fair Shares' with rows for each number of sharers (2, 3, 4, 6)

OPTIONAL: Detective Hugo Hundreds and Tina Tens — together for the capstone — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Per-group set of 12+ paper cookies (some pre-cut along third-line, some along sixth-line)
Pizza fraction cards: whole, thirds (3 sectors), sixths (6 sectors), with same-size whole pizzas for overlay demos
Lesson 5 fair-share + fraction tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Hugo brought a pizza for THREE friends. Tina brought one for SIX. How are these shares related? Ona opens: 'Same WHOLE, different SHARES!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Both Hugo and Tina puppets in hand. 'Friends — Hugo and Tina are throwing a pizza party at the Detective Agency. They have two pizzas — same size — but different friends to share with.'

Show Pizza A (Hugo's) — divided into 3 equal sectors. 'Hugo has 3 friends. He cuts his pizza into THIRDS — 3 equal pieces.' Hold up the third-divided pizza. 'Each friend gets 1/3 of the pizza.' Write 1/3 on the chart.

Show Pizza B (Tina's) — same-size pizza divided into 6 equal sectors. 'Tina has 6 friends. She cuts her pizza into SIXTHS — 6 equal pieces.' Hold up the sixth-divided pizza. 'Each friend gets 1/6 of the pizza.' Write 1/6 on the chart.

Now the equivalence reveal. 'Hugo wonders — what if I gave my friend Otto TWO of my pieces? Otto would have 2/3 of the pizza. But what if Tina gave Otto TWO of her pieces? Otto would have 2/6.' Pause. 'Are 2/3 and 2/6 the same?' Children predict.

Now the overlay move. Take one Hugo-third and place it on top of two Tina-sixths. 'Look. ONE third covers TWO sixths perfectly.' Move it to confirm. 'So 1/3 = 2/6. SAME amount of pizza.' Write 1/3 = 2/6 on the chart.

'But Hugo's slices LOOK bigger because there are fewer of them. And Tina's slices LOOK smaller because there are more of them. The pizza is the SAME — but the slice SIZE depends on how many friends are sharing.'

'Today we'll practice fair-sharing with 2, 3, 4, and 6 friends. We'll see when shares are EVEN, when we need a HALF, when we need a THIRD, when we need a SIXTH. AND we'll find more equivalences like 1/3 = 2/6.'
student_actions: Watch Hugo's third-divided pizza next to Tina's sixth-divided pizza.
Predict whether 1/3 and 2/6 are the same.

steps.instruction: Whole group: model 2 fair-share scenarios. Scenario 1: 6 cookies for 3 friends. Build with paper cookies on plates: 2 each, no leftover. Scenario 2: 7 cookies for 3 friends. Build: 2 each + 1 leftover. The leftover cookie gets cut into thirds — each friend gets an extra third. Each friend ends up with 2 and 1/3.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Two scenarios together. 6 cookies for 3 friends — share fairly.' Deal: 2 each. 'Even — no leftover.' '7 cookies for 3 friends — share fairly.' Deal: 2 each, 1 left. 'Cut the leftover into thirds.' Pre-cut paper cookie. 'Each friend now has 2 and one-third (2 1/3).' Write on chart.

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 minutes each). Station A: Even Shares — 4 share scenarios with whole-number quotients (8÷4=2, 12÷6=2, 9÷3=3, 6÷2=3). Pair deals onto plates and writes the per-plate count. Station B: Half/Third/Sixth Shares — 4 share scenarios needing a fractional split (5÷2 = 2½, 7÷3 = 2 1/3, 7÷6 = 1 1/6, 9÷6 = 1½). Pair deals, splits the leftover into the right fraction, writes the result. Station C: Equivalence Investigation — pair has third-divided and sixth-divided pizza cards. They overlay 1/3 on 2/6 and check; then 2/3 on 4/6; then 1/2 on 3/6. Write each equivalence.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each. Station B is the trickiest — match the leftover to the right fraction. Station C is about discovering equivalences. Listen for the chime.' Set the rotation.

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: include same-size pizzas divided into halves, fourths, thirds, sixths, and ninths. Discover other equivalences: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8; 1/3 = 2/6; 1/4 vs 1/3 (these are NOT equal — 1/4 is smaller).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs at Station C: 'Try to find ALL the equivalences. Some pairs are equal; some aren't. Be sure to report any pair that is NOT equal too — those are detective findings.'

steps.instruction: Circulate to record summative-style evidence on the fair-share + fraction tracker. Watch for: (a) does the child share fairly into the right number of equal groups? (b) does the child split the leftover into the right fractional pieces (third for 3 sharers, sixth for 6, half for 2, fourth for 4)? (c) can the child verbalise the 1/3 = 2/6 equivalence?
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'How do you know your share is fair?' and 'Why does 1/3 equal 2/6?' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Children whose Lesson 1-4 work was emerging stay at Station A (Even Shares) for both rotations. Anchor on 2-friend shares (halves) before extending to 3-friend (thirds) or 6-friend (sixths). The third concept can be introduced separately in a small group.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch share scenarios: 10÷4 = 2½ (using halves), 11÷4 = 2¾ (using fourths — preview of next year), 8÷3 = 2 2/3. Stretch question: 'Find a fraction equivalent to 1/2 with 8 in the denominator.' (4/8.)
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a sentence frame: 'I share ___ items with ___ friends. Each friend gets ___.' Provide picture-supported scenario cards. Pair with a strong-counter peer for Station C (the equivalence investigation).
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Dealing physical cookies onto plates is naturally kinesthetic. For movement learners, allow them to BE the dealer at every station — physically distributing one cookie to each plate. The motor act is the embodied form of fair-share. NO-MATERIALS VERSION: use 7 bottle caps (or counters/erasers) as cookies; child divides into 3 piles or 6 piles physically. Body becomes the cookie tray.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: (1) does the child share fairly with the right number of equal groups? (2) does the child split the leftover into the right fractional pieces matching the number of sharers? (3) can the child articulate the 1/3 = 2/6 equivalence?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the fair-share + fraction tracker per child as you observe.
tracker_columns: Shares fairly with right number of groups

discussion_prompts: If 3 friends share 7 cookies fairly, how many does each get? How do you know?
Why does 1/3 equal 2/6? Show with a drawing.
If you shared a pizza with 6 friends, how many SLICES would you get if you took 1/3 of the pizza?
What's the BIGGEST share — 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, or 1/6? Why?
consolidation.exit_routine: Ona's fair-shares refrain — 'Same WHOLE, different SHARES! Denominator says HOW MANY!' Class chants 3x. Each child writes one fair-share fraction with the WHOLE labeled.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Fair-share with whole-number quotients (B1.6), fair-share with fractional leftovers (B1.6 + B1.7), and the 1/3 = 2/6 equivalence (B1.7) across the 4-prompt summative worksheet plus 3-5 station observations per child.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 5 captures the B1.6 + B1.7 summative for the unit. Combined with Lessons 1-4 formative trackers, the teacher has evidence for all 7 expectations B1.1-B1.7: numbers to 200 (Lesson 1), composition + comparison (Lesson 2), even/odd (Lesson 3), estimation (Lesson 4), fair-share + fraction equivalence (Lesson 5).

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child cuts the leftover cookie in HALF for a 3-friend share — repairing the fraction-mismatch error
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On fair shares with thirds/sixths, the Grade-2 trap is the fraction-mismatch error: child treats 1/3 of 6 cookies as 1 cookie (the numerator) regardless of the whole. Empson & Levi (2011, 'Extending Children's Mathematics: Fractions and Decimals') frame this as fraction-as-quantity-of-the-whole — the fraction operates on the WHOLE, not the numerator alone.

Today integrates Lessons 1-4: place value (L1-2), even/odd (L3), estimation (L4) into fair sharing with thirds/sixths.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B (Half/Third/Sixth Shares). The child has dealt 7 cookies for 3 friends: 2 each, 1 left over. They have picked up the leftover cookie and cut it in half (using their Grade 1 strategy). They now have 2 half-pieces and don't know what to do because there are 3 friends.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Tell me about your share.' The child says '2 each, but now the half doesn't work for 3 friends.' 'Right — half worked for 2 friends because 2 friends split into 2 halves. But 3 friends need…' Pause. 'Three pieces. So we cut the leftover into THIRDS, not halves.'

Get a fresh paper cookie (pre-cut along third-lines, ideally). 'Watch — three sharers means three EQUAL pieces. THIRDS. Cut on the third-lines.' Show three pieces. 'One third for each friend. Each friend now has 2 cookies AND one-third. We write that 2 1/3.'

Now the rule. 'Hugo says — match your fraction to the number of sharers. 2 sharers → halves. 3 sharers → thirds. 4 sharers → fourths. 6 sharers → sixths. Always match.'

Have the child redo. 'Try the next scenario.' Hand the next card: 9 cookies for 6 friends. Child deals: 1 each + 3 left. 'For 6 friends, the leftover gets cut into…' '… sixths.' 'Right. 3 cookies cut into 6 sixths each = 18 sixths. Three of those go to each friend? Wait — let me think.' Together count: 18 sixths ÷ 6 = 3 sixths per friend. 'So each friend gets 1 cookie + 3 sixths = 1 1/2 (because 3/6 = 1/2).' Affirm.

If the child STILL defaults to halves: the rule hasn't connected to the WHY. Repair by going back to the pizza overlay. 'Look at the pizza divided into thirds vs the pizza divided into sixths. Each piece is sized FOR a certain number of sharers. You can't use the wrong piece.' This visual grounds the rule.

Long-term recovery: include a quick-reference card at every fair-share station: '2 sharers → halves. 3 sharers → thirds. 4 sharers → fourths. 6 sharers → sixths.' The card is the explicit anchor against the half-as-default habit.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Defaults to halves for any leftover. Stops when the half doesn't work for non-2 sharers. Most common at the start of Lesson 5 for transition learners.
(Mid) Switches to the right fraction with prompting. Doesn't yet auto-match fraction to sharers.
(Strong) Auto-matches: 3 sharers → thirds, 6 → sixths. Verbalises the rule before splitting.

(Stretched) Volunteers an alternative for non-prime sharer counts: 'For 6 sharers, I could cut into thirds, give each friend one third — wait, that's only 3 friends. Right, I need sixths.' Reasoning through the match-to-sharers rule.
common_misconceptions: The leftover always gets cut in half. (Grade-1 strategy holdover. Repair: explicit match-fraction-to-sharers rule.)

Smaller leftovers don't need cutting. (Children with 1 cookie left for 3 friends might just give it to the host. Repair: fair share means EACH FRIEND gets the same amount, including the host — no leftovers given to one person.)
Sharing into 6 means cutting in half three times. (Not wrong, but children get lost in the multi-cut process. Repair: pre-cut paper cookies on sixth-lines so the cuts are visible.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child takes numerator only (1/3 of 6 = 1): physical demo — divide 6 cookies into 3 EQUAL piles; child counts ONE pile.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child can find 1/3 but stalls on 1/6: drill 'denominator says HOW MANY equal piles'; child re-divides.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child can divide but can't articulate: force the sentence frame '1/3 of ___ = ___ because I divided into 3 equal piles.'

worksheet_brief.purpose: Summative evidence for B1.6 (fair-share with 2-10 sharers) and B1.7 (1/3 = 2/6 equivalence). Captures both whole-quotient and fractional-quotient share scenarios plus the equivalence prompt.

parts_outline.task: Two even-share scenarios. Scene A: 8 cookies for 4 friends. Scene B: 12 cookies for 6 friends. The child draws the share onto each plate and writes the per-plate count.

Two fractional-share scenarios. Scene A: 7 cookies for 3 friends (each = 2 1/3). Scene B: 9 cookies for 6 friends (each = 1 1/2). The child draws, splits the leftover into the right fraction, and writes the per-plate amount.
Equivalence prompt with two pizzas (one in thirds, one in sixths). 'Show that 1/3 = 2/6 by shading 1/3 of the first pizza and 2/6 of the second pizza.' The child shades and writes the equation.
Reasoning prompt: 'Why does 1/3 equal 2/6? Write 1-2 sentences.'
